#4138. Review: Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered (Switch 2) - The King Returns With A Fun But Thin Kaiju Brawler

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered

Godzilla fans are eating well. At the time of writing, we are on the brink of a new Toho release, a direct sequel to Goji’s first Oscar-nominated film, Minus One. There's also the next entry in Legendary's MonsterVerse to sate fans of the Western arm of the franchise (even though they have been a little Kong-heavy of late). Now, Tokusatsu mayhem is coming back to consoles, as original developer Pipeworks and Atari revamp their 2002 GameCube classic Destroy All Monsters. It smashes its way onto Switch 2 with Unreal Engine 5 visuals, online multiplayer, and some nice quality-of-life bonuses.

Destroy All Monsters Melee is a 3D arena fighter where you can choose from 12 iconic (well, maybe not Orga) kaiju and duke it out in major cities across the globe. It's an absolute joy to play for fans of the franchise, and it's accessible enough that anyone can jump in and relish the city-trampling mayhem.

There is a thin wraparound story that, while patently ridiculous, is in keeping with the lunacy of the series' Japanese entries. An alien race called the Vortaak has invaded Earth, unleashed the inhabitants of Monster Island and taken control of the kaiju that come pouring out. You play as the one friendly monster that has to battle their way to the alien mothership and take on the Vortaak's cybernetic facsimile of Earth's mightiest monster - Mechagodzilla.

That's the overarching plot, and there's only a tiny sliver of story across a couple of cinematics in the game's Adventure Mode, so don't expect a rich narrative. This game is mostly monster fights, and in this respect, it does not disappoint.

There really isn't much more to be said about the joyous spectacle of hefting Gigan over your head and hurling him into the side of a skyscraper. You can fill Anguiris with a faceful of atomic breath or fly rings around your opponent as Rodan. Destroy All Monsters Melee is filled with these moments of wonder amidst what is a fairly straightforward brawler. There are no elaborate combos here, no precise hitboxes, and no need for frame counting. There’s just multiple building-sized animals wailing on each other.

Each monster has basic punch and kick combos, coupled with powerful variants triggered by a push of the right stick. A power move knocks enemies flying at the cost of speed (Godzilla's tail whip is overpowered on any difficulty), while projectile abilities help manage distance.

Monsters can also enter Rage Mode, which lets them unleash a powerful ability that comes with an impressive visual flourish. Power-ups litter the arenas, sometimes dropped by the Vortaak’s 1950s-style UFOs. These will either top up health and special meters, or send in Mothra for an aerial bombardment. When in doubt, you can always pick up a building and throw it at your opponent.

Each monster gets its own distinct moveset, and the uniformity of the controls means it's easy to try out everyone before you settle on a main character. Godzilla is a good all-rounder, and his Millennium model is the best-looking in the game. Gigan has a powerful teleport ability that can easily bamboozle an opponent. Several monsters can fly, with Mecha-King Ghidorah in particular being a formidable combo of offence and evasion.

There are some duds, like Megalon and Orga, who have utility but just don't feel great to play. I had the most fun with Mechagodzilla (here depicted in his Heisei Kiryu form for the remaster), who combines his Maser Cannon projectile with shoulder-mounted missile salvos.

Single-player offerings include the story-driven Adventure mode, which comes in three tiers of difficulty. Survival mode has you run a gauntlet and try to last as long as possible. For pure brainless wish fulfilment, there's Destruction mode, in which one or more kaiju lay waste to a city to rack up points.

There's also a full suite of local and online multiplayer modes, including a tournament ladder to decide once and for all who gets to be crowned king of the monsters. Monsters level up in the Adventure Mode, increasing base stats and adding abilities to their repertoire, which incentivises spending time with each fighter.

The system for unlocking new arenas and monsters, which involves repeating fights in the local modes, has been updated for this remaster. Previously, the ‘research’ tied to specific unlocks was fixed. Now you can freely choose which one you want to prioritise (pro tip: unlock Ghidorah first).

That said, there isn't much to do beyond the final bit of research, and getting 100% is a patience-testing loop of the same old fights. The magic of this game is in the pick-up-and-play nature of those battles, and it doesn't stand up to laborious repetition just to view some nice artwork.

The presentation of this remaster on Switch 2 is exemplary. Monster models and arenas have all been updated, and battles play out butter-smooth both docked and undocked. Undocked in particular looks great, with those big chunky fighters and diorama cityscapes really suited to portable play. There's a real fluidity to some of the action, particularly when monsters like Gigan close the distance with incredible speed.

The audio combines lovingly polished sound effects from the movies with a cacophony of city-levelling bangs and garbled military transmissions. It's a real shame there isn't Japanese vocal audio; the early-2000s English voices really take a layer of authenticity away.

Special mention must go to Director mode, an enhanced photo mode that lets you control the camera during a fight. Adjusting the speed and setting up the perfect shot of your favourite beasts laying into each other is addictive fun. You can see why Ishiro Honda made so many of these movies.

Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a satisfyingly faithful update to a beloved Kaiju brawler. It’s simple and fun, with local and online multiplayer keeping you around for the long haul despite a wafer-thin single-player experience. Now if we could just get a remaster of Save The Earth and Unleashed…

#4137. Kojima's Xbox-Published OD KNOCK Gets A New Game Poster

Keeping up with Kojima and what he's working on is always a fun task, as we never really know what he's up to, how far along it is, when we'll hear from him again, and all that jazz.

Hideo Kojima's OD KNOCK was announced at The Game Awards in 2023, and yet we know hardly anything about the game. Last night, Kojima returned to provide us with another bump of his Xbox published OD, with a brand-new game poster.

It depicts Sophia Lillis' character looking up towards a windy red object. It kind of looks like a red broomstick, but honestly? Who knows what it is. Her character doesn't appear to be screamin' good and proper like in the previous poster, but they do share the same message: "For all players and screamers".

Sure, it's a pretty basic poster all things considered, but do you know what? It's something! Lord knows all we want is to know more about OD KNOCK and when we'll be able to understand what makes it so scary.

Earlier in the year, worries that Kojima's Xbox-published game was getting canned started to circulate, but those concerns have since been put to rest by Xbox boss Asha Sharma, who declared "to invention and adventure together with Xbox" when she visited Kojima Productions in September.

We have no idea when OD KNOCK will hit Xbox consoles, but what we do know is that when it does eventually release, we'll be here at Pure Xbox to bring you all the coverage.

#4136. Poll: Are You Happy with Your PS Plus Essential Games for November 2026?

November's PS Plus Essential games were revealed earlier this week, and I think it's quite an interesting selection.

That's because all three games offer something completely different. We've got a fairly big-name headliner, a collection of remastered adventures, and a highly-rated indie on our hands.

Dead Island 2 is up first. This punchy sequel combines hyper violent zombie-slaying with tongue-in-cheek storytelling across an apocalyptic Los Angeles.

It's a good laugh — especially if you team up with a couple of friends online — and a solid action romp.

Tomb Raider 4-6 Remastered is next on the list, and while Lara Croft's fourth, fifth, and sixth outings are rarely mentioned with the same kind of reverence as her original trilogy, they're still packed with nostalgic platforming goodness.

And last but certainly not least — go and check the review scores — is Monster Train 2. This is a deck-building roguelike full of fantastical creatures, and it's super addictive once you've wrapped your head around the turn-based mechanics.

I get it: some people hear "deck-building" and "roguelike", and they turn away — but there's a reason this hugely expanded sequel is so highly regarded.

News PS Plus Essential Games for November 2026 Announced

So, what do you make of November's PS Plus offering? As always, cast your vote in the polls, and then explain yourself in the comments section below.

#4135. A Line Held Tight is a charcoal visual novel about a miner's strike in the 32nd century and choosing your relationships wisely

We've had about roughly four decades of games as we generally know them now, and yet somehow, so often their stories feel so limited in scope. I'm not talking about a lack of big, bold ideas, in fact there might be too many of those. I more mean that there are aspects to life that often go uncovered in games. For example, when was the last time you saw a game about a workers strike? Citizen Sleeper 2 has one questline about such a thing, but it's just what the entire game is about. A Line Held Tight, a mecha visual novel about a sci-fi miner's strike, may bridge that gap.

A Line Held Tight is being developed by Humble Grove, the studio behind the quiet but impactful No Longer Home. Narrative is at the forefront with this game too, albeit with an emphasis on the choices you make throughout the strike. You play as The Canary, a member of a mining colony who's been cut off by the rest of humanity, set in the 32nd century. "As a strike boils over you’ll help The Canary to decide where their heart and their loyalties lie," the game's Steam page explains. "A branching narrative weaves its way through the deep tunnels of the mine to meet the characters within it as outside influences make themselves felt."

Those aforementioned choices you make primarily affect The Canary's relationships with friends, family and other workers, a much more appealing concept mechanically than simply different endings or storylines. In the world of labour organising, it's the relationships you build with others that's really the key thing, so it's nice to see an emphasis on that both narratively and mechanically. The game has some pretty stunning hand-drawn charcoal art too, as well as a traditional folk soundtrack, a pretty unique combo for a game.

As it stands, A Line Held Tight doesn't currently have a release date. Where it makes up for that is a demo that you can try out right now as part of Steam Next Fest, at the very least. There's a nice little video talking through some of the thought process of making a game such as this one from Humble Grove that you can check out below too. And while you're doing that, whether you check out the demo or not, perhaps give the game a little wishlist on Steam.

#4134. Genshin Impact Luna 7 brings us the first playable Hexenzirkel as things take a turn in Sumeru

Genshin Impact's Luna 7 update will kick off a new Archon Quest chapter, and deliver some interesting new additions to the playable roster.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a new Genshin Impact Special Program, where the developer revealed everything there is to know about the game’s next major update. Truth Amongst the Pages of Purana, or as its friends call it, Luna 7, was unveiled as part of the showcase.

This next update has a lot going for it, and it will be in players’ hands everywhere on May 20.

Luna 7 will take us back to Sumeru for its new Archon Quest, where a new crisis that threatens to plunge the nation into chaos is brewing. Nahida is out of the picture, and someone who looks suspiciously like Il Dottore has emerged.

If you complete this chapter at launch, you’ll earn up to 560 Primogems, as well as Nicole's Ascension Materials. Nicole is the first of three playable characters arriving with this update. Something else you’ll unlock if you finish the chapter quickly is a new Weekly Boss that HoYo says has “unpredictable abilities.”

And if you haven’t played in a while, don’t worry, you can refer to the Guiding Notes feature to catch you up on what’s been going on in the world. This is part of a larger effort from the team to make story progression more seamless, and also includes improved quest autosave prompts.

Nicole Reeyn is highest-profile and most interesting, being the first playable member of the Hexenzirkel. The mage is a 5-Star Pyro Catalyst wielder intended as a support member of the team. She can boost the ATK of all party members, even those not currently on the field. She also generates a shield while doing so.

Her Elemental Burst allows her to summon an Arcane Projection that follows the active character, sending out Coordinated Attacks that match their Elemental Type. Outside of combat, Nicole can help you find treasures by calling upon a Seelie to guide you to them. Quite fitting, as you’ll be exploring in the inside of the Witch's Lodge in Nicole’s Meeting Point in Luna 7, so bring her along.

Lohen, the Vice Captain of the Knights of Favonius' Fifth Company, is the second new character. Also a 5-Star addition, he is instead a Cryo Polearm wielder designed for aggressive combat. His main use is dealing massive Cryo DMG, and he can do that by managing two resources unique to him: Joy, and Will to Win.

Through his Elemental Skill, he can enter the Masterstroke state, allowing him to build up (and consume) Joy to unleash enhanced skills. The more his teammates fight, the more Will to Win he biulds, which can later be used to boost his effectiveness further. For an even more powerful display of force, bring along a Hexerei character when he’s on your team.

Prune is the third and final addition. Prune is a 4-Star Anemo Catalyst wielder, and her kit is inspired by her Witch Hunter aspirations. Using a bell and a hammer, she can deal DMG of several elements at once, and trigger Swirl reactions.

Nicole, and Lohen will debut in Luna 7’s first half, while Prune will follow in the second. The first half will also see a Durin rerun, with Mavuika returning in the second half. You can look forward to a new limited-time event as part of Luna 7, with a focus on Klee's Little Hexenzirkel.

You’ll find a series of mini-games you can play alongside Prune, as well as Qiqi, Yaoyao, and Sayu. If you play, you could earn the Super Awesome Magic Key, an exclusive weapon skin. Miliastra Wonderland is doing its thing, too, with a new sports festival for you to take part in.

One new gameplay addition worth calling attention to is that Manekins can now perform actions in Teyvat. The Kamera, which you can use to capture moments with Manekins, is getting upgraded, too, with new editing tools and assets.

Before you pick the game back up, be sure to check out our recently-updated Genshin Impact codes page for some free stuff you may be missing.

#4133. Mystic Messenger's most loyal players are getting banned in droves for seemingly playing the game too much

With the 10th anniversary of Mystic Messenger nearly upon us, the dating sim has inexplicably begun issuing wide-spread bans for its most active players.

Mystic Messenger, arguably one of the best dating sims around, has been dormant for about seven years. Despite not receiving new content or any meaningful updates in all that time, the game remains popular with its core fans, many of whom just woke up to some shocking news about their accounts.

The free-to-play mobile dating sim has started banning players with seemingly too many Hourglasses - the game’s virtual currency - saved up in their accounts. So far, it looks like players with 1,000 or more have been targeted, but others with far fewer hoards have reported getting the axe, too.

The news exploded on the Mystic Messenger subreddit overnight, with over a dozen reports from players logging in to play normally, only to receive an in-game notice that their accounts had been banned.

The message players received is identical, and doesn’t mention the specific reason for the ban. “Your account has been banned because abusive behavior has been detected from your account,” it reads, ending with a support email address the affected user can contact if they believe they’d banned in error.

It didn’t take a while for players to realise that most, if not all of the bans are for players with thousands of Hourglasses in their accounts. The virtual currency can both be acquired in-game just by playing, as well as through direct real-money purchases.

For a nearly ten-year-old game that stopped receiving content three years into its life, it’s easy to see how a dedicated group of players would be able to acquire so many Hourglasses by simply playing regularly for so long.

When contacted by the affected players, Cheritz, the developer and publisher of the game, has instructed them to send receipts of how they acquired Hourglasses (assuming they were purchased) to verify whether or not they’d been fraudulently obtained.

Considering that Mystic Messenger has practically been abandoned by its developer, certain exploits have emerged over the years that allowed players to farm Hourglasses faster than intended, but those instances have always been dealt with then and there.

The blanket and sudden nature of this ban is what’s spooked players, especially those who’ve been logging in for years and never thought accruing in-game currency from playing the game too much would make them the target of a ban.

The running theory is that most of the bans are unintentional, and may be the result of a new automated security system that’s been implemented. It’s entirely possible, especially if its’s AI-based, that the new system simply couldn’t distinguish between those who have earned (or bought) their Hourglasses fairly, and those who used exploits.

The timing of the ban wave is also suspect. With the game’s 10th anniversary coming up in July, it could be that Cheriz is preparing to release a large update for Mystic Messenger, which may include new content. If most of the playerbase is already sitting on massive amounts of in-game currency, they may simply use that to fast-track their way to unlocking the new content, which would greatly affect the developer’s bottom line.

This is a problem that other live service games have run into in the past. Just recently, extraction shooter Arc Raiders added a cap to the amount of Cred players can hold in their accounts very quickly after its launch. That currency is used to buy cosmetic sets in the store, so the logic is easy to follow.

All of that has certainly put a damper on the enthusiasm of the game’s most active players, many of whom were excited to get together in person for the coming 10th anniversary, participate in community nights and so on to celebrate.

It’s also disheartening to see a fanbase so loyal; playing a game as regularly for so long without new content, to be treated so poorly. Even without knowing what the game is, it’s impressive that so many people have kept the flag of their favourite game flying for so long.

#4132. Report: EA Bet On Star Wars Battlefront III Success, Cancelled Mass Effect Was Too 'Risky'

Looks like we're getting another Battlefront game!

It looks like a collective decision was made at EA to shut BioWare down and focus on the biggest opportunities for the future.

According to a report from Bloomberg, EA execs met up to review their upcoming portfolio and were tasked with deciding which of two multi-million dollar sci-fi franchises to prioritise, opting for Star Wars Battlefront III and cancelling a new Mass Effect title.

"While this is never easy, we ultimately have to make tough decisions to focus our teams on the biggest opportunities for our future, including investing in new projects across our portfolio,"

The decision was made to ensure a more comfortable prediction for success, hedging its bets on Battlefront III being the less risky option between the two.

"As they reviewed EA’s portfolio for the next few years, the company’s executives found themselves with two sci-fi action games that were each projected to cost hundreds of millions of dollars: Star Wars Battlefront III and the next Mass Effect title. They chose to invest in Star Wars and shut down BioWare as a result, said the people familiar, speaking anonymously because they were not authorized to talk to the press.

Star Wars Battlefront III has not even begun development yet, but EA executives saw it as a less risky, more predictable bet than a new Mass Effect — and the publisher behind Battlefield has always been more comfortable with shooters than RPGs."

The report goes on to share some other reasons as to why execs were worried about BioWare and Mass Effect. Namely, how EA saw Mass Effect: Andromeda, Anthem, and Dragon Age: The Veilguard as financial letdowns, with the latter "missing sales expectations by 50%".

Star Wars Battlefront III was just the source of rumours and speculation a few weeks ago, but now it seems like EA execs are ready to go all-in on another Force-sensitive shooter. The game still isn't in active development yet, with rumours swirling that previous Battlefront developer DICE isn't a firm lock on the project, and that Disney has even considered a pitch from Marathon and Halo creators Bungie for the new entry.

#4131. Cyberpunk 2077's new dual wielding has already been modded to include shotguns and rifles, provided you're down to get "janky and wildly overpowered"

It was only ever going to be a matter of time, but I'm still surprised just how quickly Cyberpunk 2077 modders have taken pistol dual wielding mechanic the RPG's Edgerunners 2 update has just added in, and opened it up to include any gun Night City has to offer. Yep, twinning shotguns, assault rifles, sniper rifles, or any combo of those is now possible. Though, you'll have to make peace with the fact enemies will struggle to match your firepower.

A number of different modders instantly decided to take on the task of extending the tag which governs Cyberpunk's new dual wielding perk to include everything with a trigger. There's Dual Wield Anything by long-time Cyberpunk modder E3roKK, Dual Wield Anything and Everything for 2.5 by Jollywankers, and Expanded Dual Wielding by JericoHellden. All three have been released within the last 24 hours.

JericoHellden's mod also includes the option to control each gun separately, rather than CD Projekt Red's default of automatically alternating between the two when firing. If you're only interested in twinning pistols, but do want the ability to independently fire each gun, another new mod - Independent Pistol Controls (Dual Wielding) by Dederara - might be for you.

Here are clips showing Jollywankers' (directly below) and Dederara's (the further down of the two) works in action:

It's worth noting that, in line with the reason CD Projekt Red gave for limiting it to pistols in their official update, dual wielding other guns without any measures in place to make enemies tougher does blunt the challenge of fighting your way through Night City. JericoHellden declared it a "janky and wildly overpowered" experience, and E3roKK made clear that anyone expecting animations not to get a bit clippy or awkward at times is barking up the wrong tree.

If you're hoping to dual wield katanas, unfortunately it looks like melee weapons will take a bit more time to figure out properly, with some of these mods including them only as a 'try it but don't expect things to work yet' afterthought to the ranged main course. Makes sense, given the official integration is designed for lead slingers rather than slappy cybersticks.

The latest version of Cyber Engine Tweaks, the framework mod needed for any Cybeprunk mod setup that's not limited to the likes of light visual tweaks, is a requirement for all for of the mods mentioned here. Redscript is also needed for Expanded Dual Wielding.

#4130. Rumour: Days Gone Dev to Announce and Launch New PS5 Game in 2027

Third-person game with co-op, it's reported

Bend Studio, the first-party team best known for Days Gone, plans to reveal and potentially even release its next game in 2027.

That's according to a new MP1st report, which shares more details on the project. The outlet claims an announcement will take place next year and it's "much further along in development" than you might think, so much so that Bend Studio is also planning to release it in 2027.

MP1st calls the project a third-person experience with co-op features, but it's not a live service title.

The website also claims it won't be a sequel to Days Gone. Previous reports stated Bend Studio pitched a Days Gone 2 to Sony after the first game, but it was turned down. It then actually did turn its attention to a Game as a Service, though this was cancelled at the start of last year.

Now, according to the outlet, Bend Studio is gearing up to announce and release its project next year. With Until Dawn 2, God of War Laufey, and potentially also Intergalactic slated for 2027, it could be a busy 12 months for Sony's first-party developers.

This is just the latest report from MP1st surrounding PlayStation's unannounced plans. It has also suggested a Killzone project is in the works, and teased what to expect from Media Molecule next.

Rumour Killzone Project in Early Development, Probably a Remake

Rumour Media Molecule's Next Game Is Out Next Year and Unlike Anything It's Made Before

With a new PS5 title around the corner, Bend Studio is indeed best known for Days Gone, as its biggest and most recent project. However, the developer has been part of Sony for over 20 years. @EfYI No one is saying 'woke', 'progressives' or 'PC' or anything else is a new concept, it isn't. What we are strongly pushing back on is the idea that it was because of reviewers political views that they gave Days Gone an average score (72 on Opencritic), this is misguided.

Days Gone reviewed lower than it should have is because the game was buggy as hell at launch. Most reviews stated they had issues, everything from texture pop-in, audio dropouts, audio-sync issues, cutscene glitches and more. Some even lost progress. It isn't the same game you played later. Push Square gave it 7/10.

The remaster, where these issues were fixed, scored far more fairly at 81 on Opencritic. 8/10 feels about right for me. It's a good game with a few exceptional moments (horde), but also too many other things holding it back. Reviews also mentioned structural bloat, repetitive open-world missions, an overly fragile bike, auto-fail stealth missions, and a predictable, uninspiring story. That is all fair criticism.

If you liked it more than that, good for you, but suggesting it is due to reviewers political opinions is just looking for an excuse to validate your own preferences. It's OK to like a game more, or less, than an average review score. It doesn't have to be something deeper.

FWIW I agree with you on the horde system, it's fantastic. The problem was it was mostly only relevant in small doses in the game, mostly towards the endgame. That was when the game was at it's very best. But to get there you had to slog through a lot of pretty average open world content to see it.

Personally I was looking forward to a sequel. With the groundwork laid I thought they could build on that to make much better game with fewer weak areas. It's a shame that never happened.

#4129. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Switch 2 Development Team Has Been Revealed

Nintendo has just released the first two parts of a new Ask the Developer series all about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2. Alongside a bunch of interesting insights about the game's development, the interview also finally reveals the development team behind it.

As it turns out, the Switch 2 remake was developed internally by Nintendo's Entertainment Planning & Development (EPD) Production Group No. 3 — the team that has handled just about every Zelda entry since the early 2000s.

The remake saw HokWai Ng take on the role of Director (his first Dir. role at the company, though he also worked on Tears of the Kingdom), with Aya Shida (Pikmin 3, Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, Tears of the Kingdom) on Art Direction, Hiroki Taguchi (Breath of the Wild) as the Program Director, and Masato Ohashi (Animal Crossing: New Horizons, Splatoon 3 Expansion Pass) as Music Lead and one of the Sound Directors.

There was a part of us that thought Nintendo might bring in another studio to work on the remake — particularly as it increasingly appeared more and more faithful to the original — but it's nice to see that it was an inside job instead. Worry not, Zelda legends Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi both served as producers on the project.

Parts three and four of the OoT Ask the Developer series will be released tomorrow (3rd November), so we're sure that there are even more dev stories to come. Gosh, what a week to be a Zelda fan!

#4128. Forza Horizon 6 explodes on Steam even before it's officially out

Forza Horizon 6 looks to have easily delivered the most successful launch for any game in the series on PC, with record-breaking player numbers.

Steam is abuzz this week with a couple of long-anticipated launches, but in Forza Horizon 6’s case, at least, the game isn’t even out for what will be most of its players. The anticipated sequel in the open-world driving game series doesn’t officially launch until May 19, but owners of its most expensive version - the Premium Edition - can play it right now.

That version of the game includes more than just a few days of early access, of course, but you’d think the $120 price tag would’ve only been palatable to a small group of players. Not the case with this game.

Forza Horizon 6, which has spent 16 weeks in Steam’s global top sellers list, currently occupies the number two spot, having jumped up three spots this week in anticipation of the launch. The game has also naturally been popular with players, so popular in fact that it has already overtaken the player counts of all other Horizon games on the platform.

At the time of writing, the game has peaked at 128,157 concurrent players on Steam alone (via SteamDB). The figure has already climbed several times during the writing of this story, so you can only imagine how much higher it’s going to get deeper into the weekend.

All of that, of course, days before the official launch on Tuesday, when, theoretically, the majority of the game’s audience will be able to start playing. In just a few short hours, Horizon 6 has already gone well above Forza Horizon 5’s peak concurrent of 81,096, as well as Forza Horizon 4’s peak 75,689 players.

Steam is the only platform that publishes player numbers, of course, but it’s easy to see how similar the enthusiasm is going to be on Xbox. Though the game is not yet part of the Game Pass line-up, those who don’t want to wait could buy the Premium Edition Upgrade to get the included content, and play it right now.

Game Pass, and Xbox / Windows Store numbers don’t factor into Steam’s, which is another thing to consider when viewing the numbers holistically. Indeed, given how successful Forza Horizon 5 has been on PlayStation 5, Horizon 6’s upcoming release on Sony's console is bound to be even bigger.

Forza Horizon 5 has been off to a similarly flying start in the first few days of its own advanced access launch, so it’s obviously not surprising to see Horizon 6 do better there. In case you missed it, check out our review of Forza Horizon 6. In short, we really liked it, even if we expected more.

#4127. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.3 will take us deeper into the World in Canvas and make Mortenax Blade playable

Honkai: Star Rail's next big outing will see the continuation of the Planarcadia story, and it's going to be with us soon.

HoYoverse has today delivered full details on the next major update for Honkai: Star Rail. Version 4.3, dubbed The Lethe Below the Living, will be available for all players on June 1. The upcoming update adds a new chapter to the Planarcadia arc, and introduce a new playable character.

The new narrative chapter will also unveil more about Mortenax Blade, the Trailblazer themselves, and the husk of the Aeon.

Mortenax Blade is the hero of this chapter, and he’s going to step into the World in Canvas. The goal is to - by borrowing the power of Voracity - excise Shuhu from his body and end the curse.

The Trailblazer goes on a trip of their own in Version 4.3, this time to Inkford Hermitage, right on the edge between the World in Canvas and the real world. They’re going to undertake this journey to warn Graphia of the Asat Pramad threat.

In case you hadn’t already guessed, Mortenax Blade is this version’s new playable character. The 5-Star Fire-Type swordsman is on the Path of Nihility. Blade’s Ultimate allows him to enter an enhanced state by deploying a special Bounded Field.

While the field is active, all enemies receive more DMG. Entering this state is also how Blade unlocks his skill, which uses a Sword Formation to deal more damage. This is then used to essentially unlock a second, more powerful Ultimate for him.

The benefits of Mortenax Blade’s kit extend to his teammates, too. Any ally who attacks an enemy with him on the team, they inflict a debuff on them. This also builds up a special Charge that Blade can later use with his Skill.

Version 4.3’s launch arrives alongside the Gift of Tempered Blade event. Through it, you can claim a new Trailblazer Outfit piece for free, but only after getting Mortenax Blade from Warping. The first phase’s rerun will be Yao Guang, and the second phase will bring back both Cyrene and Phainon.

You can also expect the Wispae Amusement Park to arrive within the World in Canvas, which you’ll get to design. You can plan where the rides will go, pick the different themes, set visitor routes and more.

Starward Mode is another new addition, which can be found in Memory of Chaos, Pure Fiction, and Apocalyptic Shadow. Starward will see you take on three different stages, which you’ll need three teams for. Clearing each challenge with full stars will reward you 100 Stellar Jades extra per chase.

There’s more coming down the line, too. A new Fate/Stay Night [Unlimited Blade Works] collaboration will arrive in a content up this summer. The event will give players a chance to earn Gilgamesh or Archer for free by logging in.

#4126. "What if Larian had shut down after Divine Divinity?": Star Trek Online exec scorns publishers who close teams like BioWare in favour of "AAA veteran" start-ups and AI "magic beans"

It's like "setting fire to millions of dollars of property and equipment"

Breaking up established game development teams in favour of "AAA veteran" start-ups and "magic bean" technologies is like "setting fire to millions of dollars of property and equipment", in the words of Star Trek Online executive producer Thomas Marrone. He thinks it's "wildly irresponsible and self-sabotaging", and that videogame company shareholders should be absolutely furious about it.

Marrone's comments come in response to EA closing BioWare yesterday, but he takes aim at closures and layoffs across the industry. He notes that many of the most successful teams owe their accomplishments to lessons learned from screw-ups, and suggests that if big game publishers just want "number to go up", they should get out of the game-making trade and pour all their cash into investment funds.

"One of the most insightful comments about game development came from a former boss," Marrone wrote on Bluesky this morning. "He said 'Making a game is like starting a band. You can’t throw money at a new studio with random AAA veterans and expect it to crank out a hit.' A good game needs a vision. A good game needs a good team to build it. A good team needs chemistry to work well together. Team chemistry needs years of collaboration to gel. There are certainly 'rockstars' and leaders who are anchors for their team, but they need to have that chemistry and trust with everyone around them to be truly effective.

"The AAA philosophy seems to be to hire four random musicians and expect them to become the Beatles overnight," Marrone went on. "When it does happen: well, we have the songs now, we can just hire different musicians to record new songs when we want another album. It’s truly insane and shows a fundamental misunderstanding of the collaborative creative process at the heart of making games.

"Most studios that generate an overnight hit are actually on the 3rd or 4th title," he said. "Blizzard, Larian, Arrowhead, these places had several games under their belts before their first true blockbuster. Like George RR Martin they had been grinding XP for years before becoming a household name. The current AAA Publisher practice of disbanding studios, even if they ship a game successfully, is so counterintuitive to their own financial future it boggles my mind.

"Like if I were a major shareholder I would be livid," Marrone observed. "This is wanton destruction of these publishers’ most precious assets. It’s like literally setting fire to millions of dollars of property and equipment. It’s wildly irresponsible and self-sabotaging. If big game publishers just want number to go up, fire everyone and just invest it all in mutual funds or something. If you don’t want to actually make a product, and you don’t want to build a business around making a product, just liquidate your assets and stop pretending you want to make anything."

Marrone has been at Cryptic Studios for 16 years, starting out as an associate graphics designer. "I've worked on one game through that whole career, which means I've seen lots of leaders come and go, and lots of versions of the company and the game as it grew, shrunk, and changed," he noted.

Cryptic themselves were founded in 2000, and are also known for Champions Online, City of Heroes and Neverwinter. They've been through a lot of upheaval lately. Cryptic were acquired by (*dread bell tolls*) publishing conglomerate Embracer in 2021, during the latter's early-Covid-era campaign to absorb half the industry. When Embracer belatedly acknowledged that all of their acquisitions had left them up shit creek without a paddle, Cryptic Studios were among the many subsidiaries who had to lay off staff. Then, Embracer sold them to Project Golden Arc, a new company formed by former Star Trek Online publishers Arc and XD Inc, publishers of Torchlight: Infinite and Heartopia.

I'm not sure how many of Cryptic's founding staff are still there, but Marrone makes it sound like they've done a fair job of keeping their teams together. "I have very personal experience working on a team that has gone through all the corpo speak stages 'forming, storming, norming, and performing,'" he wrote. "It can take Y E A R S to get to that final stage. When you do, it's awesome. People are 2, 3, 4x as effective as when they start. But it just. takes. Time."

"It takes time to build a team," Marrone went on. "It takes shared experiences. It takes shared wins AND shared losses. What if Larian had shut down after Divine Divinity? What if Arrowhead had shut down after Magicka? What if Hello Games had shuttered after the initial launch of No Man's Sky? These studios have all had ups and downs but they were given time to grow and learn and their teams got better and better. Not to say those teams were static, but certainly there was a continuity and culture that informed their biggest successes.

"And when you look at the arc of a studio like Bioware, you can begin to see how important it is to keep the teams healthy, how important it is to keep those rockstars and leaders together with the teams that know them," he said. "Mass Effect is a great game. Mass Effect 2 is one of the best games of all time.

"In my current position I understand the pressure of leadership when millions of dollars and hundreds of salaries are at stake," Marrone concluded. "I understand the drive to find a magic bean like NFTs or GenAI or whatever is trending on LinkedIn this week. There's got to be a 'trick.' We've got to find a 'trick.' But." Marrone ends the thread by reiterating the need to "nurture and empower your team".

We've heard plenty of common-sensical commentary like this from other senior devs of late. In April, Bit Reactor boss and former XCOM developer Greg Foertsch spoke to Julian about how he and other Firaxis managers "kept the team together" across development of Sid Meier's Railroads, XCOM: Enemy Unknown, and XCOM 2.

We've also recently seen a number of new "AAA veteran" startups come and go, as investors take fright after an initial buzz of interest during the Covid lockdown period. Former BioWare manager Casey Hudson launched a new studio in 2021 only to shutter the company in 2024. Former Mass Effect and Dragon Age scribe Mac Walters similarly launched a company in 2023, only for publishers NetEase to pull funding a year later. There are going to be a lot more BioWare veterans in the wilds this year, joining many thousands laid off by the likes of Microsoft and Ubisoft.

#4125. Three Special Football Jerseys Go On Sale To Celebrate Xbox's 25th Anniversary

I've always been a big fan of wearing sports merch - you'll find me sporting a Vancouver Canucks hoodie or jacket most days of the week! However, when I was looking around for some kind of Xbox jersey in preparation for the Xbox FanFest event in London last month, I was disappointed to find basically nothing except old Seattle Sounders shirts.

That's all changed this week, as Xbox has teamed up with a company called Dyenamik to produce three Xbox "Jerseys" to celebrate the brand's 25th anniversary, all of which are now available to buy.

You can either purchase them individually (for £70 here in the UK with worldwide shipping available), or grab a special bundle of all three for £175 with a collector's box, although that one's limited to just 200 people.

So, let's go through them - here's a look at all three:

The black body carries a tonal X across the front and back, shaded in darker panels to echo the raised X on the original console's casing. The sleeve displays the original XBOX logo graphic while the retro wordmark takes pride of place on the jersey front. Neon green piping runs along the raglan seams, complimenting the vibrant accents in the collar and cuffs.

Please note that some external links on this page are affiliate links, which means if you click them and make a purchase we may receive a small percentage of the sale. Please read our FTC Disclosure for more information.

A pure white jersey with XBOX green panels sweeping down the body, finished with a banded silver pixel pattern. The green collar and double-striped cuffs are complimented with silver piping along the raglan seams. Across the chest is the XBOX 360 wordmark in its original green and grey. The XBOX sphere is embroidered in green on the left chest and the Dyenamik emblem sits on the right. On the back, just below the collar, is the comforting visual of a green Ring of Light.

Look into the green stripes and you'll find tonal hardware detailing: circuit-board traces, vent grilles, and port outlines, layered green on green. The pattern is inspired by the semi-transparent XBOX consoles that let you see the components inside the shell. Up front is the modern XBOX wordmark in white, with an embroidered XBOX sphere on the left chest and the Dyenamik emblem on the right. On the back, just below the collar, sits the A, B, X and Y button layout, an XBOX signature and a configuration that's felt like home for 25 years.

Twenty-five years of XBOX, in one drop. The Anniversary Collection brings together all three Dyenamik XBOX heritage jerseys, the X, the 360 and the ABXY, and crowns the set with the strictly limited XBOX Collector's Box. Three eras of the console you grew up with, made to wear and made to keep.

So, there we go! I'm personally a big fan of the mostly black Xbox design, but I bet many people will be drawn to the Xbox 360 version, or maybe the ultra-colourful third jersey.

£70 is a lot for a shirt, but any kind of sports merch seems to be competitively priced these days, and I don't believe there's anything else like these on the market. A fun little partnership for sure!

#4124. Nintendo Wanted To Remake Ocarina Of Time To "Trigger New Insights" For Future Titles

"Hang on, why is Nintendo remaking Ocarina of Time again?" It's a natural question that might have occurred to you in the last few months, and in the latest Ask the Developer interview, Series Producer Eiji Aonuma had the answer.

Part of the reason for returning to the title, it turns out, was to try to "trigger new insights" from the developers that may feed into future Zelda games. "Many of the team members who work alongside me on Legend of Zelda games today have only experienced developing the more recent titles," Aonuma-san says. "That led me to wonder, 'Do they truly understand just how significant The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was to the series as a whole?'"

"I started to wonder how they'd interpret The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as they go about developing future Legend of Zelda games," he continues. "By learning the game structure and development style behind the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and by actually rebuilding it as a full remake, it may trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development."

While he describes the potential behind such insights as "extremely valuable," he also notes that it wasn't the only reason he wanted to return to OoT for the series' 40th anniversary. The game's structure is drastically different from more recent series entries like Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, two games that a whole generation of Zelda fans will have grown up on (as sobering a thought as that is), so Nintendo wanted to showcase a different style of gameplay, too:

In The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, part of the fun comes from progressing through a carefully paced adventure and story, gradually building up the player’s growth and their understanding of the narrative along the way. We wanted players who had grown accustomed to Legend of Zelda games like Breath of the Wild, where they can freely choose their own path from the start, to experience that kind of gameplay as well

Whether revisiting Ocarina of Time actually does influence any future games' design decisions remains to be seen, but if you're looking for GoodGameTM inspiration, it certainly isn't a bad place to start.

The Ask the Developer interview also revealed that Ocarina of Time was internally developed at Nintendo, with HokWai Ng in the Director's seat.

#4123. Monopoly Go x The Simpsons crossover is almost here

After a long wait and exhaustive leaks, the highly-anticipated Simpsons event will finally arrive in Monopoly Go very soon, alongside new content.

Monopoly Go players have been looking forward to a major crossover event for what felt like months, and though most of the details ended up leaking, nothing actually beats official information.

The world of The Simpsons has officially arrived in Monopoly Go, and there's a whole lot for players to dive into. The show's creative team even produced a new animated short, featuring Mr. Monopoly, and Mr. Burns.

Available June 3 through July 29, the new event allows Monopoly Go players to jump in the world of The Simpsons. You'll be able to build, and explore all around multiple iconic locations from the show.

Along the way, you'll run into Simpsons characters like Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa, and of course, Mr. Burns. Developer Scopely teamed up with the show's creative team to create many references, and Easter Eggs for you to discover. You'll find some of those on chance cards, but most of the world has been changed to be part of The Simpsons, including getting to bribe Chief Wiggum to escape jail.

The developer promises a deeply connected world with Simpsons narratives and characters that alter seasonal maps, and offer unique sticker sets and animated sequences to dive in. Incidentally, this is The Simpsons' first appearance in a mobile-exclusive game in 13 years.

Here's a breakdown of everything you can expect, straight from Scopely:

Episodes: Narrative-driven encounters that create stories inspired by The Simpsons. Episodes play out across seasonal boards, sticker sets, and minigames, all capped off with an animated short.

Sticker sets: Every Episode comes with its own limited-time sticker set, taking cues from the latest Simpsons story. Collectible artwork, character journeys and other rewards are yours to claim for the duration of each Episode.

The Simpsons Run: Every two weeks, a new Springfield character will take over the Free Parking tile, kicking off character-driven runs.

Simpsons-themed Shutdowns and Heists: Monopoly Go's shutdowns and heists get a Simpsons makeover, with Springfield-inspired chaos and disasters.

Bribe Wiggum: This changes Go to Jail to allow players to bribe Chief Wiggum, giving you a chance to earn a bigger reward, but not without introducing an element of unpredictability.

Simpsons chance cards: The chance card collection grows with over 50 Simpsons-themed cards full of memes, references and one-liners from the show.

If you're excited to jump in tomorrow, be sure to check out these Free Monopoly Go Dice Links before you dive into the new content.

#4122. Half-Life 3 speculation reignited by Valve dev mentioning three sweet little rumored codenamey letters amid technical chat about video game noises

Wake up. There's Half-Life 3 chatter occurring again. This time because, about an hour into a panel about sounds in video games, a Valve composer has uttered three eyebrow-raising letters. HLX. In an industry rife with acronyms, what's so special about this one? Well, it's a rumoured codename for the next entry in the aforementioned series about a man with a crowbar, for one.

"Basically, that's one of the three pieces that come together to make HDR that you can easily optimise," Valve music designer Mike Morasky said during a panel at GameSoundCon, answering a regular old question about the techincal ins and out of managing sound in games. The panel had been running for about an hour when he said this, so clearly nothing that'd get people out of their seats was in the offing.

"In fact, I think Deadlock has their own version of HDR," he continued. "HLX has its own version, so on and so forth." AHA, voices screamed around the world. He said the thing. HLX, in case you're not on top of the list of acronyms that should set you off yapping about Valve games, previously appeared in a data string from a Counter-Strike 2 update and looks like it could turn out to be a codename for a future game from Gabe and co. That's going off Half-Life: Alyx's codename having been HLVR.

If it was HLXXX, I imagine one would have to assume it to be a possible codename for a Gordon Freeman sex tape or a Half-Life collaboration with Vin Diesel, star of the 2002 film XXX. I don't know about you, but either would excite me greatly.

Morasky's co-panelist David Feise doesn't look to have been subtle in sarcastically pointing out the former's slip of the tongue to him via some cheeky whispering while the two were still up in stage. Morasky also looks to have plenty of form for this sort of tongue slippage in relation to HLX.

Does any of this tell us anything other than potentially confirming once more that Half-Life 3 exists? No, but hey, it's something. One thing we do know is that ex-Valve writer Chet Faliszek has said that he wouldn't be interested in helping pen a Half-Life 3 if indeed one is hiding in the ether to catch out musicians whose mouths sometimes move faster than their brains (as happens to all of us).

#4121. Rumour: Alleged Persona 1 Remake Gameplay Leaks Online

Alleged footage of a Persona 1 Remake has emerged online, although in this age of AI generated content it’s incredibly difficult to ascertain whether this is legit or not.

My jerk reaction is that it’s probably real, as it appears to include reused animations from the unreleased Persona 4 Revival. A similar leak occurred prior to the official announcement of Persona 3 Reload.

But as always, you should take this with a pinch of salt.

The video shows combat featuring characters from Persona 1, alongside Persona 2’s protagonist Tatsuya Suou.

Series producer Kazuhisa Wada has spoken quite candidly about how Persona 1 and 2 remakes are something Atlus should “eventually do”, so this project has been an open secret for some time now.

It’s worth noting that Persona 4 Revival is due out on 17th February, so even if this footage is real, I wouldn’t expect two remakes in the same year. It’s probably still a little way away.

#4120. Helldivers 3 "only makes sense" if it’s so unlike Helldivers 2 "that both games can exist side by side", says Arrowhead boss, discussing their new prototype game

95% of studio still on Helldivers 2, with a "small team" on the next game

Arrowhead Game Studios will only make a Helldivers 3 if it's lightyears apart in style from Helldivers 2, or if Helldivers 2's playercount falls through the floor. This is my takeaway, at least, from a recent chat with Johan Pilestedt, chief creative officer, in which Pilestedt touched briefly on the studio's next unannounced game, while assuring me that there are still no plans for a Helldiver threequel.

According to Pilestedt, 95% of the studio is focused on Helldivers 2, with a "small team" now prototyping Arrowhead's next game. They currently have around 150 people on the books. "Studio-wise, we want to grow on our own terms and know when to stop," Pilestedt commented over email, noting that "plenty of teams hit big and immediately double their size".

As for the prospect of Helldivers 3, Pilestedt is wary of dividing the audience while Helldivers 2 still has a following, commenting that "for now, my view is that a sequel resets everything and forces players to start over", whereas "a continuation turns the game into a lifelong hobby, like LEGO or Warhammer". In what probably isn't a sign that he's getting David Lynch to direct the next Warbonds video, he framed Helldivers 2 "as a 'third space,' a community where people can spend a huge amount of their time, but equally one that players can go away from for months or years and still find fun and community when they come back." For context, Helldivers 2's Steam live playercount as of writing is 47,097, which isn't chart-topping but seems fairly respectable for a two-year-old game; this doesn't include console players, of course.

"Some studios can treat players like a short-term cash grab," Pilestedt went on. "We see players as the actual engine of the game: they're the ones bringing in friends, making memes, and keeping the game alive. When you have an active community doing that, you don’t need a sequel.

"The industry is panicking because the old live-service tricks don’t work anymore," he said. "And the biggest competitor to a Helldivers 3 would be Helldivers 2. It only makes sense to make a distinct sequel if it’s so different that both games can exist side by side. For now, making Helldivers 2 better every day makes way more sense than throwing away its momentum."

Pilestedt didn't spell out what he meant by the industry panicking, but I assume he's referring to all the live service game cancellations of late. 'Live service' in general – aka, turning games into platforms from which 'rents' can be extracted, be it an optional cosmetic purchase or a subscription - has become something of a cussword among players who'd rather their games were less online, habit-forming and, well, landlordy.

The intrigue here, for me, is just how different Helldivers 3 would need to be to stand apart from its predecessor. Helldivers 2 is a very different game from the original Helldivers, swapping the old top-down view for third-person gunnery with a greater emphasis on physics and credible weapon handling. Where should they go next?

I'm not sure Helldivers would be entertaining as a first-person shooter – so much of the game's beguiling daftness depends on seeing your character. I could well imagine a Helldivers RTS, but that'd probably be a spin-off project. There are other directions they could take within the third-person shooter genre that might change the feel while supporting the game's brash and callous dystopian humour. God, I almost typed the words "Helldivers battle royale" there. Close one!

#4119. Rumours Persist That Xbox Spent $500 Million On Gears Of War: E-Day, Despite Some Objections

Update #3 [Mon 2nd Nov 2026, 1pm]: Yet more updates continue to trickle out! To avoid clogging up this original article too much, we've covered the newest information in a separate article elsewhere on Pure Xbox:

News Former Xbox Manager Explains Why $500M Cost For Gears: E-Day Doesn't Tell The Whole Story

Update #2 [Fri 30th Oct 2026, 7:30pm]: In yet another update on this, Bloomberg's Jason Schreier has weighed in on the rumour.

Schreier was discussing BioWare's recent closure when he threw out the Gears of War mention:

"The reality is that BioWare was shut down for the same reason that game companies have been laying off tens of thousands of people over the last few years, which is that game budgets have grown exponentially and become more and more expensive for these companies to make.

We just saw Gears of War: E-Day cost $500 million to Xbox. That is a real number, that is real. That's what we're looking at here - that's what games cost to make, especially in North America these days."

Both Chris Dring of The Game Business and Jez Corden of Windows Central have shared their updated thoughts on this today, with Jez now suggesting that the $500 million figure is correct but he's still not sure how it's distributed.

Original Story: Ever wondered how much money went into Gears of War: E-Day's release this year? Well, we don't have any official figures on this, but a "source" for Kotaku has claimed that Xbox put over $500 million into it.

Their report claims that it's a "source familiar with Xbox’s business", and that the $500 million figure doesn't actually include marketing for the game either. Microsoft apparently didn't respond when asked for comment on this.

Here's a look at the bit from the report in question:

"But according to one source familiar with Xbox’s business, the cost of Gears of War: E-Day is in fact much higher. They told Kotaku it was over $500 million, and that’s before you include marketing."

Kotaku says this makes it significantly higher than the reported budgets of other console exclusives this generation, such as Marvel's Spider-Man 2 which was rumoured to cost around $300 million.

However, not everyone agrees. A few months ago, Insider Gaming journalist Tom Henderson stated on a podcast that he'd heard Gears of War: E-Day cost "upwards of $400 million", which he described as "insane".

Windows Central's Jez Corden then acknowledged this on the Xbox Two podcast, explaining that the $400 million wasn't just for Gears of War: E-Day, as The Coalition works on many other games (Forza, Fable) and even beyond games ("the technological glue for all of Xbox") and some money "is spread across the entire portfolio". He advised that you "can't say" Gears of War: E-Day had a $400 million budget, and that it's "not even the case".

"The $400 million is not all Gears E-Day. You've got to remember that The Coalition is the technological glue for all of Xbox. They don't just work on games, they work on dev tools, they work on Unreal Engine, they work on a lot of stuff beyond simply Gears of War. Some of that money is spread across the entire portfolio. And it's not just the Unreal games either - The Coalition has contributed to Forza, to Fable, to everything. You can't really say 'Gears: E-Day has a $400 million budget'. That's not even the case."

Ultimately, we're not going to get an official answer unless Microsoft / Xbox comes out and says how much the budget was, and that seems unlikely at this point. The figures that are being quoted are certainly extravagant, but we're inclined to believe what Jez is saying about the budget being spread across far more than just one single game.

In any case, we absolutely love Gears of War: E-Day, awarding it a rare 10/10 score at launch!

@theduckofdeath I’m not sure I agree about scale. Sony, for example, report on ALL their divisions regardless of the size. Furthermore this reticence by Microsoft to hide and obfuscate figures has been widely reported for decades outside of Xbox. It’s a Microsoft thing. (And also an American Company thing)

I also disagree that no one cared before. Were you not alive during the 8-bit and 16-bit console wars, they were in many ways far more polarising than the current 3 horse race, people absolutely did care how Sega v Nintendo were doing. Though I agree it was less about financial targets and more “mine is better than yours, it sold more, scored higher, or has better graphics”.

Yet the reality is we live in a different time, back then a studio could output a game every year, or several a year with much fewer staff and a relatively small budget. A game could fail, or several games could fail in a row, and your studio would often keep going regardless. That isn’t the case now. There are REAL stakes involved now, and failure could mean the end of a company you love (RIP BioWare et al) or an IP you want to see more of. There’s a totally valid reason it is different now.

I also agree SOME people will just use it to console war - that is both sad and undeniable true - but many of us want to know because it directly affects us when these companies or games do poorly and we no longer get to see games and IP love, and see the brilliant creators of our hobby out of work. The game will be marked as breaking even after sales and gamepass revenue allocation. It wont' turn a profit, but Xbox is just laying ground work for the next gen.

The whole plan will be to find away to get an affordable next gen system out the door, with going back to full console exclusive outside of the Activision/Blizzard brand. The whole thing will be about getting bigger franchises out the door quicker, and passion projects are done. Creatives shouldn’t be running studios for the most part, that was Phil's biggest downfall. Giving creatives too much freedom, just burns money.

No one at Xbox is naive to believe this gen is salvageable. The cost of laying ground work for the future is a loss they are willing to take right now.

I'll copy my comments from other articles here:

E-Day is definitely in trouble if you just look at Steam. Its peak high for the past 24 hours is just 7,565, which for a game of its scale, that cost so much, and which only came out a couple of weeks ago is truly terrible. Oh, and just by way of comparison, Helldivers 2 had a peak high of 46,648 over the same period, and that game came to Steam February 2024, added to which, that 24 hour peak high is 15,000 higher than E-Day managed at its peak! So yes, E-Day is in significant trouble, and I say that as someone that absolutely loved the Campaign, and also bought the Collector's Edition.

Obviously Game Pass could well be a factor on both PC and Xbox, but I imagine that even with that, the drop off will be similar to that seen on Steam where it started with a peak high of about 31,500. In other words, Steam has seen something like 75% fewer people playing the game now than occurred when the game first released just two weeks ago, and I imagine that it will be much the same among those of us that bought the game on Xbox, and also Game Pass on PC and Xbox.

Losing 75% of your gamers in the space of 2 weeks is not good.

As for The Coalition, bearing in mind that Sharma still needs to find over 1000 job cuts, I think they will suffer badly, and go someway to addressing her redundancy problem.

I expect The Coalition to be cut to the bare minimum, with just enough people to do a year of seasons for the game (which will then just be repeated every 3 months just as happened with Gears 5, which is still having seasons to this day). Once work on any DLC and the seasonal work is complete, I expect them to switch to finishing the PlayStation version, where it will likely release either the end of next year, or the beginning of 2027. Basically, I think The Coalition will become a zombie studio, mortally wounded, and probably done for within 2 years. E-Day could easily be the last game we get. I know that sounds totally apocalyptic, but you cannot make a game costing upwards of half a billion, and sell so few copies, and have a 75% drop off of players within the first 2 weeks. Whether the existing community will hang around and keep playing, and crucially, keep spending in the game, I'm not sure. When you see such a significant drop in player numbers so quickly after release, it does not usually bode well for a game (or a studio)...

Microsoft's biggest problem, as I've seen it over the decades, is that they often seem to lose patience.

They invests heavily, expects the market to respond, and when dominance doesn't materialise quickly enough, they change direction, restructure or abandons the project altogether.

That's particularly damaging in gaming, where customer loyalty and confidence take years to build

Mobile: Windows Phone couldn't overcome Apple's and Google's established ecosystems

Music: Zune was a decent product, but Apple owned the market with the iPod/iTunes

Web browsers: Internet Explorer dominated, then Microsoft lost ground to Chrome and Firefox

Search engines: Bing has struggled to dislodge Google, despite Microsoft's enormous resources.

Gaming: Xbox entered as a serious competitor, but Sony and Nintendo continued to maintain stronger identities and customer loyalty.

Microsoft has the resources and cash to compete with almost anyone. What it seems to struggle with is accepting that having deep pockets doesn't mean it gets to dictate the market.

As I've said before, Xbox as an ecosystem can survive, but hardware? I'm not particularly hopeful for the future of Helix.

@BAMozzy yes costs are a factor, something I accepted much earlier in this exchange, doesn't stop gamepass cannibalising sales to the point that revenue from gamepass doesn't cover that shortfall. @Llamageddon And sales is NOT the ONLY revenue option - if SALES was the ONLY method to generating revenue, ONLY way to measure a games Success, they wouldn't put their games into a service that would hurt sales figures.

But that doesn't change the fact that Game Pass Revenue exceeds the running costs of the Studios.

You are the one who decided to be argumentative and respond to my post with your OPINION that was totally unnecessary and I certainly didn't appreciate your continued argumentative and unreasoned approach. Its really not difficult to understand that Gamers across the world are not spending as much money, because they don't have as much money to spend which means that SALES aren't as high as needed - especially as Rising Costs require more and more Sales to break even and why Publishers have had to make Cuts across the entire industry, why Studios have been closed. That doesn't mean EVERY Game will be a Flop just that Publishers are NOT receiving the amount of Sales revenue they hoped and/or needed to keep the Studio they had as running costs escalate - less and less money coming in whilst costs rise means Jobs and studios close - its a SIMPLE concept and has been how businesses have operated for generations. @FraserG Derek Reese, former Senior Product Manager at Xbox, explained on Bluesky that a large portion of this amount was not solely related to the game's development itself, but rather to costs associated with Xbox's internal branch of Unreal Engine, as well as broader technology work that benefits not only Gears of War: E-Day but the entire Xbox studio ecosystem.

In short, it's basically an accounting issue. The engine costs are being charged to The Coalition, when in reality they should be shared across the other studios that also benefit from that technology.

So, to put it bluntly, most of the articles published over the last few days, and even Jason Schreier himself, were talking nonsense.

I'm not talking about the comments here, where most people are speaking out of ignorance. That's not really their fault. However, when it comes from so-called insiders, it's much more serious and significantly undermines their credibility.

@Fiendish-Beaver 'PlayStation, which has become completely complacent in the face of limited competition.' I was well aware of the comment by Reese, and it has been mentioned by a few others, @fatpunkslim, so I most certainly am not speaking from a position of ignorance. The truth is we will never know precisely how much the game cost (or indeed how much it makes and loses), but you only have to look at the product we are presented with to know that we are looking at a game that easily cost $200 million to make, and probably more than $300 million. You simply cannot make a game of the quality of E-Day for anything less than that.

Equally, we can look at Steam to see that E-Day dropped to just 6,832 24 hour peak high on a Saturday night, down from a peak high of 31,000 in just two weeks. That is a drop off of 78%, which is not good. Not good at all. And yes, I am still not ignorant to the demanding nature of the game on PC.

Neither a budget that is north of $200 million, nor the poor sales on PC, will save The Coalition now. It has not made anywhere near enough revenue to prevent large scale job loses at the studio, which is something I really, really do not want to happen. I may not be a fan of what The Coalition have done with "Horde", but I still want them to make another game (and the rumoured single player content that they have in the works, and also the rumoured game based on the Pendulum Wars, albeit how a game without Locust will fare, I'm not too sure).

What I will say is that I know full well that we are being told that the $500 million is not correct, but we are also led to believe that this $500 million does not include the publicity and advertising that the game received, which has been spoken about in terms of a frankly unbelievable further $500 million (and I used the word 'unbelievable' advisedly because I quite literally do not believe it). However, the point remains that we are led to believe that the rumoured $500 developmental costs do not include the games publicity, though of course (as is usual with Xbox and Microsoft) we will never know any facts because it does not suit them to tell us.

Regardless, no one can paint E-Day as a success other than in terms of its quality, and that alone will not save it. My only hope in all this is that The Coalition survives and is able to make another game in the franchise, and do so within a timely manner. If the axe falls too heavily, it will trim the studio to the bone, leaving them just enough staff to make the seasonal content (and probably finish the PS5 version! 😉), but incapable of getting another game out the door for many years if at all...

I think it will be PlayStation's best year this generation, @Llamageddon. Another God of War game, Intergalactic and a game rumoured to be releasing from Bend studio. As you say, it would be just like Sony to do this right at the end of a generation to persuade you that it is indeed worth investing in the next generation console...
